newsitem.title: GERMANY: German jobless surges to new post-war record.
newsitem.headline: German jobless surges to new post-war record.

text.p: German unemployment surged to a new post-war record of 4.66 million, or 12.2 percent, in January, reaching levels last seen in the depths of the Great Depression of the 1930s.

A massive rise of half million new jobless -- due in part to a harsh weather that saw large numbers of construction workers laid off -- raised concern about the country's sputtering economic recovery and Bonn's ability to meet European monetary union requirements.
It also dashed many economists' hopes that unemployment would fall later this year and sharpened pressure on the Bundesbank central bank to cut interest rates.
"January's unemployment numbers are truly hideous," said HSBC James Capel analyst Stephen King in London.
The unemployment rate, based on unadjusted data, rose to 12.2 percent from 10.8 percent in December, the Federal Labour Office said Thursday.

On a seasonally adjusted basis the number of unemployed workers rose by 160,000 from December to 4.317 million in January, or 11.3 percent of the workforce, smashing the consensus view among economists of a 52,000 rise.
As a result, Bonn will face higher unemployment benefit costs than it had planned for in a budget tightened to meet European monetary union requirements, economists said.
"There is a high risk Germany will not meet the 3 percent gross domestic product-to-defict ratio target," Joerg Kraemer, a Merrill Lynch economist in Frankfurt, said.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel's bid to cut the defict to 2.9 percent of GDP assumes stable unemployment in 1997.
Economists at Trinkaus Capital Management said that view was "no longer tenable" and raises "uncertainty and speculation about the stability of the government."
But Labour Office chief Bernhard Jagoda predicted more people would get back to work when the weather improves.

"This figure cannot be made to look good, but it should also be recognised that the situation in January contains seasonal unemployment, and it follows that in spring we can reckon with a clear reduction," Jagoda told reporters.

A Labour Office official said he expected unemployment to average between 4.1 million and 4.2 million this year, but admitted the number could rise if 1997 economic growth falls below Bonn's projection of 2.5 percent.
